item.research_question: How can high-entropy alloy (HEA) nanoparticles be synthesized continuously and scalably directly from pure elemental metal powders without using metal salt precursors?
item.material_system: CrFeCoNiMo, CrMnFeCoNi, MnFeCoNiCu, and CrFeCoNiCu high-entropy alloys synthesized from elemental metal powders (Cr, Mn, Fe, Co, Ni, Cu, Mo)
item.processing_route: Continuous feed of equimolar elemental metal powders (1.2–2.0 g min⁻¹) into a 45 kW, ~3 MHz induction plasma jet at 66.7 kPa; vaporization in core (>8000 K) followed by rapid quenching (10⁵–10⁶ K s⁻¹) using Ar, Ar-H₂ (8.3% H₂), or Ar-He (77.4% He) plasma gases; collection via cyclone separator and porous filter (2.8 μm pore size)
item.test_conditions: Synthesis at 66.7 kPa with plasma power fixed at 45 kW; optical emission spectroscopy at Z=0.23 m and Z=0.49 m; thermal stability tested by annealing at 1173 K (900 °C) for 72 h in flowing argon; optical absorption measured via diffuse reflectance spectroscopy from 250 to 2500 nm
key_findings: Achieved continuous synthesis rate approaching 35 g h⁻¹ with a conversion efficiency of 42% for CrFeCoNiMo HEA NPs.
Produced spherical HEA NPs with average sizes of 39.7 ± 20.3 nm (Ar-He) and 60.8 ± 30.1 nm (Ar-H₂).
All synthesized HEA NPs exhibited a single FCC crystal structure despite constituent elements having BCC or HCP structures in bulk.
HEA NPs demonstrated excellent light absorption with average absorptance >96% over a wide spectrum (250–2500 nm).
HEA NPs remained thermally stable after annealing at 1173 K for 72 h, with minimal dealloying or segregation.
Mo composition in products was lower than feedstock (e.g., 5.2% in HEA-He vs. 20% in feed) due to Mo's low saturation vapor pressure.
HEA-He samples showed higher crystallinity (crystallite size 17.93 nm) compared to HEA-H₂ (17.08 nm) due to faster cooling rates.
item.mechanism: The authors propose that the high-entropy effect (increased mixing entropy and decreased partial pressure of individual elements) prevents pure metal nucleation despite large nucleation temperature gaps. For hydrogen plasma, the mechanism is predominantly Vapor-Liquid-Solid (VLS) transformation where Mo nuclei form first, followed by co-condensation in the liquid phase allowing diffusion-driven alloying. For helium plasma, the mechanism is predominantly Vapor-Solid (VS) transformation due to rapid cooling, leading to direct solidification with less amorphous content but potentially higher element segregation.
item.limitations: The low saturation vapor pressure of Mo leads to incomplete evaporation and compositional deviation (Mo loss) in the final product. Unvaporized feedstock powders (up to tens of μm) are generated and must be removed, reducing overall yield. Compositional variation exists among particles (up to 8.4% for HEA-H₂) due to size distribution. Cu segregation was observed at particle edges in CrFeCoNiCu systems due to positive binary mixing enthalpies.
item.future_work: Optimize processing parameters (feed rate, plasma power, powder injection geometry) to improve Mo evaporation and compositional uniformity. Investigate direct solar energy absorption experiments with the produced HEA NPs. Explore reactor geometries with rapid jet expansion or thermal insulators to control particle size and residence time. Study the effect of using nano-sized Mo powders to ensure better evaporation without altering the thermofluidic field.
quotes: Here, we propose an ultrafast (< 100 ms), one-step method that enables the continuous synthesis of HEA NPs directly from elemental metal powders via in-flight alloying.
The HEA NPs demonstrate an excellent light absorption of > 96% over a wide spectrum, representing great potential for photothermal conversion of solar energy at large scales.

item.research_question: How to extract light absorptance spectra from high-entropy alloy nanoparticle samples and how reactor geometry and plasma gas composition affect the thermofluid field during synthesis?
item.material_system: High-entropy alloy (HEA) nanoparticles (HEA NP) and elemental metal feedstock
item.processing_route: Diffuse reflectance spectroscopy using a Perkin Elmer Lambda-900 spectrophotometer with a 15 cm diameter integrating sphere; samples crushed into 1 cm diameter pellets; CFD simulations using an in-house plasma code coupled with ANSYS-FLUENT based on magneto-hydrodynamic (MHD) theory and the Reynolds stress model; DFT simulations using VASP with PAW method, GGA-PBE, 520 eV cutoff, and 100-atom supercells
item.test_conditions: Pellets measured with a 1 cm diameter aperture; scan rate reduced from 240 nm min−1 to 6 nm min−1 above 2000 nm and around 810 nm; DFT calculations performed at 8 different lattice constants; plasma gas properties calculated under local thermodynamic equilibrium (LTE) assumption
key_findings: Diffuse reflectance (Rd) was calculated as Rd = (Is-I0)/(I100-I0) where Is is sample measurement, I0 is aperture reflectance, and I100 is spectralon standard.
Absorptance (A) was extracted using A = 1-Rd because transmittance (Td) was null for the opaque pellets.
Thermodynamic and transport properties of plasma gases were calculated under the local thermodynamic equilibrium (LTE) assumption.
Vaporization of feedstock was not taken into account in CFD simulations due to lack of thermodynamic and transport data for metal vapors in the 1000 − 10,000 K range.
Ten different random configurations for a given phase and composition were generated and examined using the hybrid Cuckoo search code.
Spin-polarized calculations were performed for both BCC and FCC phases using 100-atom supercells.
item.mechanism: The authors explain that absorptance is derived from reflectance measurements on opaque pellets, while the thermofluid field is modeled using MHD theory and the Reynolds stress model to account for turbulence, though feedstock vaporization is excluded due to missing data.
item.limitations: The vaporization of feedstock was not taken into account due to the lack of thermodynamic and transport data of some metal vapors for a wide range of temperature of 1000 − 10,000 K.
quotes: The absorptance A was directly extracted using A = 1-Rd + Td = 1-Rd, where Td is the transmittance, null is our case (the pellets were opaque).

Although powder injection and its vaporization are important phenomena to study, the vaporization of feedstock was not taken into account due to the lack of thermodynamic and transport data of some metal vapors for a wide range of temperature of 1000 − 10,000 K.
Ten different random configurations for a given phase and composition were generated and examined.
